processing: A way of drinking tea, not a factory style. Tea is roasted in a small clay pot, boiled with water into a strong brew, then poured into a cup holding baijiu, which makes a sharp crackle.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; it is made from whatever tea the household has.
appearance_dry: Ordinary local tea, darkened by roasting in the pot.
appearance_liquor: A dark amber brew, as expected from strong pot-roasted tea, cut with clear spirit.
appearance_wet: Scorched, dark leaf left in the pot, as with other pot-roasted teas.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record exists. Expect strong roasted tea with bitterness and the heat of grain spirit.

brewing.notes: Roast the leaf in a warm clay pot, add water and boil to a thick brew, then pour it into a cup with a small measure of baijiu. It contains alcohol, and the cup can spit.

vintage_note: Never sold as a product or by year. It is made at home from everyday tea and baijiu. Any current tea does the job, and nothing is documented about a preferred season or age.
description:
Longhudou, dragon and tiger fight, is a Naxi way of drinking tea from around Jade Dragon Snow Mountain near Lijiang. In Naxi it is recorded as a-ji-le-kao (阿吉勒烤). The fight of the name is tea against strong spirit.

Tea is roasted in a small clay pot, then boiled with water into a strong brew. That hot brew is poured into a cup with baijiu in it, and the crackle it makes is taken as a good omen: the louder, the happier the company.

Expect something strong, toasty and warming. Some households add a chilli, and folk belief says that sweating it out helps a cold. That is a folk belief and not a remedy worth relying on.

It is worth trying for the ritual, with a small measure of spirit. A related salted version replaces the baijiu with salt.
history: Little is documented beyond popular accounts of Naxi customs, which place the practice around Jade Dragon Snow Mountain. No date or originator is on record.
